Seattle, Washington · bring the bike

Should you bring your bike to Seattle?

Bring it.

The short answer, in full

Delta, Southwest and American check a packed bike as an ordinary bag, $45 each way as your first bag (Oct 2026). Once you land, Link light rail runs from the airport to downtown in 38 minutes. If the trip is a day or two, Métier on Capitol Hill rents a Cervélo or a Tarmac for $125 to $175 a day and evo in Fremont a carbon road bike for $100 (Oct 2026). For a week, or the STP, ride your own. No Seattle shop says on its site it receives a shipped bike. You don’t need a car: the Burke-Gilman, the Lake Washington loop and the Bainbridge ferry all start in the city, and Amtrak Cascades has ten $5 bike racks on every train for the ride home from Portland.

Fly itShip itRent oneGet aroundThe rules

Flying to Seattle with a bike

  1. Seattle-Tacoma International (SEA)

    • 14 mi from Seattle

    About 14 miles south of downtown.

    More about SEA

    Link light rail leaves from the parking garage: find baggage carousel 16, go up one floor to the skybridge level, cross Skybridge Six and turn left through the garage to the station; a free electric shuttle covers the same walk. Trains every 8 to 10 minutes most of the day, 38 minutes to downtown; Sound Transit’s night bus runs about every 30 minutes from about 15 minutes after the last train (Oct 2026). Ride apps pick up on the 3rd floor of the garage, stalls 1 to 34 on the Ground Transportation Plaza, per the Port of Seattle (Oct 2026). Check the airport’s own site for which airlines fly here.

What the airlines charge

Read on each airline’s own page, Oct 2026.

Airline by airline

Delta: a non-motorized touring or single-seat racing bike must be packed in a durable container built for bikes; the standard baggage allowance and fees apply, excess-weight fees over 50 lb; over 115 linear inches or 100 lb is refused; a soft bag or anything but a hard shell means signing a limited release; some Delta Connection carriers don’t take bikes. First bag $45, second $55, US domestic Main, each way. Southwest: a non-motorized single-seat bike is checked baggage at standard checked-bag and overweight fees with oversize fees waived; over 100 lb or 115 inches total is refused; pedals and handlebars off and wrapped; cardboard or soft cases fly only with a limited release. First bag $45, second $55 for travel booked on or after April 9, 2026; 51 to 70 lb is $100 on top, 71 to 100 lb $200. American (read Oct 3, 2026): one non-motorized bike in a hard case, bike bag or bike box pays the standard checked-bag fee up to 50 lb and the standard overweight fee from 51 to 70 lb; oversize fees don’t apply; nothing over 70 lb or 115 linear inches; handlebars fixed sideways and pedals off, or both wrapped; outside a hard case it’s treated as fragile. First bag $45 online or $50 at the airport, second $55 or $60 (fees updated May 18, 2026). Alaska: read its sports-equipment page before you book; Cascade’s STP transportation page says sports equipment including your bike is standard checked baggage with no additional fees (read Oct 2026), and the Los Angeles guide’s Sept 2026 read of Alaska’s own page said the same, $45 first bag, oversize waived, overweight waived to 70 lb. Confirm on alaskaair.com before you book. United: not confirmed; its page needs JavaScript. Keep the case under 50 lb and on Delta, Southwest and American it is one ordinary checked bag.

Shipping your bike to Seattle

How shipping works here

No shop in Seattle says on its own site that it receives a bike shipped to the shop, so call before you book a BikeFlights label with a shop as the address. Two publish a build fee for a boxed bike: Mello Fellos downtown, $190 ($250 for an e-bike); Cascade Bicycle Studio in Fremont, $250 and up (both Oct 2026). Métier’s tailored builds start at $895 for a frame from any maker, not a boxed-bike rebuild. Ask Mello Fellos or Cascade Bicycle Studio whether they’ll sign for the box. BikeFlights’ shop FAQ says some shops pack and book the shipment for you and others ask you to book once they’ve packed it (read Oct 2026); its shipping policy points to UPS’s and FedEx’s guides and gives no transit-day count. For the STP, Cascade’s 2026 transportation page carried a BikeFlights code, STPCLASSIC, 15% off through Aug 12, 2026; watch the 2027 page for the new one.

Renting a bike in Seattle

Seattle rents real bikes, gravel included.

What renting costs and what you get

Métier on Capitol Hill has a Cervélo Caledonia (Ultegra Di2) or Soloist (Ultegra) at $125 a day and a Specialized Tarmac SL8 or Cervélo Aspero gravel bike (SRAM Rival AXS) at $175, 10% off from four days, your choice of pedals, no helmets to rent, closed Mondays (Oct 2026). evo in Fremont rents a carbon road bike for $100 a day or $500 a week, helmet included, with no model named (Oct 2026). Mello Fellos downtown rents road and gravel bikes with helmet and lock but publishes no price; Ride Bicycles in Issaquah rents mountain and e-mountain bikes for the Tiger Mountain trails, reservations required, no price on the page (Oct 2026). Nobody lists sizes on their own page; call with your height. The math: flying the bike costs $90 round trip as a first bag on Delta, Southwest or American (Oct 2026), so one day on a Métier bike is a wash and two days costs more than the case. From three days, a fit you depend on, or the STP’s 206 miles, bring yours. Montlake Bicycle Shop near the STP start rents city, electric and mountain bikes, no road bikes.

Getting around Seattle with a bike

You can skip the car.

Not for most of it.

Getting around, in full

The Burke-Gilman and the West Seattle loop start in the city, the north-lake trail loop can start at UW Station on Link, the Bainbridge Island loop starts at Colman Dock downtown, and the Lake Washington loop passes Seward Park, so you can join it there. Two rides sit out of town: the Zoo Hill climb from a Bellevue park and the gravel loop from Carnation in the Snoqualmie Valley; for those, a car or a long ride out. The Bainbridge ferry: $11.35 for an adult plus a $1 bicycle surcharge, paid at Seattle only, nothing to pay coming back ($5.65 for 65 and over, under 19 free; fares for Oct 4, 2026). Be there 20 minutes early: bikes load onto the forward end of the car deck and unload ahead of the cars; arrive late and you wait at the rear and leave after them. You can leave the bike on the car deck during the crossing; take your bags, and don’t get off without it. The STP starts at the University of Washington’s E-18 lot, parking $20 a day Friday to Monday, cash preferred (2026). Getting home from Portland, Cascade sold Bus & Bike for $115 and Bike-Only for $70 by July 5 (2026 prices, the overview page); buses load at the DoubleTree finish on NE 9th Ave Saturday night, Sunday afternoon and Monday morning, standby cash only ($100 bus and bike, $60 bike only). A personal bike box rides Seattle to Portland one way ($20 on the transportation page, $25 on the overview, 2026). Or take the train: Amtrak Cascades has ten bike racks in the baggage car on every train, $5 each, booked as a bicycle space with your ticket; e-bikes under 50 lb are fine; if the racks are sold out, boxing is $15 a box plus a $10 handling fee at staffed stations only, and you take the bike apart yourself (read Oct 2026). Book the bike space early in summer. Portland-based riders: the Portland Bicycling Club runs a Friday bus and bike truck to the UW dorms, sold as an add-on at registration (2026).

  • Transit: Link light rail: roll the bike on, free, first come first served.
Transit and bike share, in full

Transit: Link light rail: roll the bike on, free, first come first served; a bike up to 84 inches long, 23 inches wide and 50 lb; no bikes when a car holds more than double its seats; never on an escalator, use the stairs or elevator; e-bikes powered off, no charging, UL-certified batteries (Sound Transit, Oct 2026). Sounder: up to 70 inches long, tires to 3.25 inches, 75 lb. ST Express buses: wheelbase to 48 inches, tires to 3.2 inches, 75 lb. King County Metro buses carry three bikes on the front rack, load and unload at any regular stop; most e-bikes are too heavy for the rack and cargo bikes too long (Oct 2026). The King County Water Taxi to West Seattle and Vashon has racks for 10 to 26 bikes depending on the boat. Bike lockers at most transit centers, park and rides and rail stations, booked through the BikeLink app. Washington State Ferries: standard walk-on fare plus a $1 to $4 stowage surcharge by route, waived with a multi-ride or ORCA card except on the Anacortes and San Juan routes; bikes board the forward end of the car deck and leave first (Oct 2026).

The rules on the road in Washington

Washington law, from WSDOT’s bicyclist laws page (modified Sept 26, 2025.

Every rule, in full

Read Oct 2026). Drivers passing a bike must move fully into the left lane or slow to a safe speed and pass at a safe distance, at least three feet where practicable (RCW 46.61.110). Stop signs are yield signs for cyclists, the Safety Stop, except at railroad crossings and school-bus stop signals (RCW 46.61.190). No statewide helmet law; local rules exist (Pierce and Spokane counties in unincorporated areas). E-bikes: Class 1 and 2 (20 mph) may use shared-use paths; Class 3 (28 mph) may not use shared-use paths or non-motorized trails and stays off sidewalks (RCW 46.37.690). Two abreast is legal, not three (RCW 46.61.770). Sidewalk riding is allowed with a pedestrian’s duties unless a city bans it (RCW 46.61.755). After dark, a white front light visible 500 feet and a red rear reflector visible 600 feet (RCW 46.61.780). The honest read: SDOT’s preliminary 2024 data showed zero bicyclist deaths and ten pedestrian deaths, half the 2021 peak (Seattle Bike Blog, March 2025); its 2026 Vision Zero update said the city is not on a path to zero by 2030 and that 80% of pedestrian collisions happen on streets with multiple lanes in the same direction (Seattle Bike Blog, April 2026). The high-injury network is the arterials: Aurora Ave N, Rainier Ave S, Lake City Way, MLK Way S, Denny Way, 4th Ave S, Northgate Way. Ride the trails and the neighborhood greenways between them, and cross the arterials at lights.
